source_text:
Epistula ad Theodosium imperatorem
Τοιγαροῦν ὁμολογοῦμεν τὸν μονογενῆ υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ θεὸν τέλειον,
ὁμοούσιον τῷ πατρὶ κατὰ τὴν θεότητα καὶ ὁμοούσιον ἡμῖν τὸν αὐτὸν κατὰ τὴν
ἀνθρωπότητα. ∆ύο γὰρ φύσεων ἕνωσις γέγονεν, ὅθεν ἕνα Χριστόν, ἕνα υἱόν, ἕνα
κύριον ὁμολογοῦμεν. Καὶ εἰ δοκεῖ, δειξώμεθα εἰς παράδειγμα τὴν καθ' ἡμᾶς αὐτοὺς
σύνθεσιν καθ' ἣν ἐσμὲν ἄνθρωποι. Συντεθείμεθα γὰρ ἐκ ψυχῆς καὶ σώματος καὶ
ὁρῶμεν φύσεις δύο, ἑτέραν μὲν τοῦ σώματος, ἑτέραν δὲ τῆς ψυχῆς, ἀλλ' εἷς ἐξ
ἀμφοῖν καθ' ἕνωσιν ἄνθρωπος καὶ οὐχὶ τὸ ἐκ δύο φύσεων συντεθεῖσθαι δύο
ἀνθρώπους τὸν ἕνα νοεῖσθαι παρασκευάζει, ἀλλ' ἕνα ἄνθρωπον. Ἐὰν γὰρ ἀνέλωμεν
τὸ ὅτι ἐκ δύο καὶ διαφόρων φύσεων ὁ εἷς καὶ μόνος ἐστὶ Χριστός, ἐροῦσιν οἱ δι'
ἐναντίας· εἰ μία φύσις τὸ ὅλον, πῶς ἐνηνθρώπησεν ἢ ποίαν δὲ ἀνεποιήσατο σάρκα;
Τοὺς δὲ λέγοντας ὅτι κρᾶσις ἢ σύγχυσις ἢ φυρμὸς ἐγένετο τοῦ θεοῦ λόγου πρὸς τὴν
σάρκα, τούτους ἀναθεματίζει ἡ καθολικὴ καὶ ἀποστολικὴ ἐκκλησία.
thought_title: Confession of one Christ from two natures
orientation: Cyril opens his letter to the emperor by confessing the orthodox faith about Christ, then answers an anticipated objection.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore we confess the only-begotten Son of God as perfect God, consubstantial with the Father in divinity and the same one consubstantial with us in humanity. For a union of two natures has occurred, from which we confess one Christ, one Son, one Lord. And if it seems good, let us offer as an example the composition in ourselves by which we are human. For we are composed from soul and body, and we see two natures, one of the body, another of the soul, but one human being from both by union, and being composed from two natures does not make the one be thought of as two human beings, but as one human being. For if we take away the fact that the one and only Christ is from two different natures, our opponents (the opposite side) will say: if the whole is one nature, how did he become human, or what flesh did he take to himself? Those who say that a mixture or confusion or blending of God the Word with the flesh occurred, these the catholic and apostolic church anathematizes.

choices.why: Fixed glossary term for sharing the same being; avoids banned alternatives.
Fixed glossary term for the union of divine and human natures in Christ.
Fixed glossary term for the putting together of soul and body as an analogy.
Fixed glossary term for the rejected mixing of the Word with the flesh.
Fixed glossary term for the rejected merging of the Word with the flesh.
Fixed glossary term for the rejected jumbling of the Word with the flesh.

pass_b_english: We confess, then, that the only-begotten Son of God is perfect God, consubstantial with the Father in divinity and consubstantial with us in humanity. A union of natures has occurred, and from this we confess one Christ, one Son, one Lord. If it seems good, let us take as an example the composition by which we ourselves are human. We are composed of soul and body, and we see two natures, one of the body and another of the soul, yet the one human being from both in union does not make us think of two human beings because he is composed from two natures, but one human being. For if we do away with the fact that the one and only Christ is from two different natures, our opponents will say: if the whole is one nature, how did he become human, or what flesh did he take to himself? As for those who say that a mixture or confusion or blending of God the Word with the flesh occurred, the catholic and apostolic church anathematizes them.

last_rejected.quote: yet the one human being from both in union does not make us think of two human beings because he is composed from two natures, but one human being
last_rejected.source_quote: ἀλλ' εἷς ἐξ ἀμφοῖν καθ' ἕνωσιν ἄνθρωπος καὶ οὐχὶ τὸ ἐκ δύο φύσεων συντεθεῖσθαι δύο ἀνθρώπους τὸν ἕνα νοεῖσθαι παρασκευάζει, ἀλλ' ἕνα ἄνθρωπον
last_rejected.why: Subject flipped: Greek says 'one man from both... does not make the one be thought as two', English says 'does not make us think of two human beings because he is composed from two natures'.
last_rejected.fix: yet one human being from both in union, and being composed from two natures does not make the one be understood as two human beings, but one human being.
last_rejected.ruling: Greek τὸν ἕνα νοεῖσθαι παρασκευάζει = 'makes the one be conceived'; 'us think' is natural English for νοεῖσθαι; meaning preserved.

last_rejected.why: English adds 'our' not in source, and masks the formal marker οἱ δι' ἐναντίας ('those on the opposite side').
last_rejected.fix: those on the opposite side will say
last_rejected.ruling: οἱ δι' ἐναντίας = 'those on the opposite side'; 'our opponents' is standard equivalent; 'our' is minor, not misleading.

last_rejected.quote: how did he become human, or what flesh did he take to himself?
last_rejected.source_quote: πῶς ἐνηνθρώπησεν ἢ ποίαν δὲ ἀνεποιήσατο σάρκα;
last_rejected.why: ἐνηνθρώπησεν is 'became incarnate/man', not 'become human'; ἀνεποιήσατο is 'assumed/took', not 'take to himself'.
last_rejected.fix: how was he incarnated, or what flesh did he assume?
last_rejected.ruling: ἐνηνθρώπησεν = 'became human/incarnate'; ἀνεποιήσατο = 'made/assumed for himself'; renderings within normal range, no meaning lost.

problems.why: Same group called two different names; reader may think they differ.
problems.fix: Use 'opponents' consistently or gloss as 'our opponents (the opposite side)'.

problems.quote: if the whole is one nature, how did he become human, or what flesh did he take to himself?
problems.why: Objection lacks clear closing marker; reader may miss return to Cyril's voice.
problems.fix: Add closing quotation marks or 'they say' before 'As for those who say'.

problems.quote: our opponents will say: if the whole is one nature, how did he become human, or what flesh did he take to himself?
problems.why: Reader may not grasp that this is an objection Cyril is raising hypothetically, not his own statement.
problems.fix: Mark the objection more clearly as an opponent's challenge or rhetorical question.

problems.quote: As for those who say that a mixture or confusion or blending of God the Word with the flesh occurred, the catholic and apostolic church anathematizes them.
problems.why: Reader may confuse this group with the opponents just quoted; these are a different group teaching mixture, not separation.
problems.fix: Clarify that this condemns a different error (confusion) from the one just discussed (separation).

edits.old: our opponents will say: if the whole is one nature, how did he become human, or what flesh did he take to himself?
edits.new: our opponents will say: “If the whole is one nature, how did he become human, or what flesh did he take to himself?”

edits.old: As for those who say that a mixture or confusion or blending of God the Word with the flesh occurred, the catholic and apostolic church anathematizes them.
edits.new: As for those who say that a mixture or confusion or blending of God the Word with the flesh occurred—a different error—the catholic and apostolic church anathematizes them.

fixed: The speaker problem about the objection lacking a clear closing marker was fixed by adding quotation marks around the objection.
The speaker problem about the objection not being clearly marked as an opponent's challenge was fixed by the quotation marks and the existing phrase 'our opponents will say'.
The speaker problem about confusing the group teaching mixture with the opponents just quoted was fixed by adding '—a different error—' to clarify that this condemns a different group.
